Thousand
thou'zŭnd
n. and a. (ten hundred; in Scripture the standard figure for an uncountable abundance and for a divine reckoning of time)
From Anglo-Saxon thusend, akin to the Gothic thusundi, thought to mean a swollen hundred — the hundred grown past holding. The Hebrew eleph is the same idea from the other side: it is also the word for a clan or a company, so that a thousand in Israel is not first a figure but a body of men.

Biblical Definition

The thousand is where Scripture's counting passes out of the reader's hand and into God's. It measures His ownership: “every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psa 50:10) — a rebuke to any worshipper who imagines he supplies God with anything. It measures His relation to time: “a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past” (Psa 90:4), which Peter takes up and turns both ways — “one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (2Pe 3:8). Moses uses the thousand to shrink man; Peter uses it to explain God's apparent slowness, which is longsuffering and not delay. And in the Hebrew census the eleph is a fighting company, so that Israel's thousands are ranks of real men under real captains. The thousand is therefore never merely large: it is the point at which the creature's arithmetic gives out and the Creator's does not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a thousand as the number of ten hundred, and notes at once its proverbial use to signify a great but indefinite number.

expand to see more

THOUSAND, n. The number of ten hundred.

2. Proverbially, a great number, indefinitely.

THOUSAND, a. Consisting of ten hundred in number.

2. Proverbially, denoting a great number. He is one of a thousand.

Key Scripture

Psa 90:4 — "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."

2Pe 3:8 — "But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day."

Psa 50:10 — "For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills."

Rev 7:4 — "And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel."

Modern Corruption

Psa 90:4 and 2Pe 3:8 are pressed into service as a formula for converting the Bible's days into geological ages — a use neither text will bear.

expand to see more

Neither verse offers an exchange rate. Moses is contrasting the everlasting God with grass that withers before evening; Peter is answering scoffers who mistake God's patience for slackness, and he says the thousand and the day are alike to the Lord in both directions — which is a statement about God's relation to duration, not a coefficient for reinterpreting Genesis 1. Taking the phrase as arithmetic requires ignoring the word as, which is a simile and not an equals sign.

The other misuse runs the opposite way, taking the thousand years of Revelation 20 as an exact civil calendar to be plotted against current events. The dictionary holds the millennial question open among amillennial, postmillennial, and historic premillennial readings, and rejects the dispensational chart-making that turns the number into a schedule. What Psa 50:10 settles is more urgent than either dispute: the God who owns the cattle upon a thousand hills is not enriched by our offerings and not impoverished by our withholding.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew eleph (H505), a thousand — also a clan, family, or military company; Greek chilioi (G5507), a thousand, and chilias (G5505), a company of a thousand.

expand to see more

Hebrew eleph (H505) — a thousand; the same consonants also give alluph, a chief, and the word for a clan — a thousand in Israel is a body of men before it is a figure.

Hebrew sar alaphim — “rulers of thousands” (Exo 18:21), the highest rank in Jethro's ordering; the thousand is the largest unit a single man is given to shepherd.

Greek chilioi (G5507) — a thousand; the thousand years of Rev 20.

Greek chilias (G5505) — a group of a thousand; the twelve thousand of each tribe in Rev 7.

Greek chiliarchos (G5506) — a chief captain over a thousand, the officer who rescues Paul in Act 21:31-33.

Usage

"“The cattle upon a thousand hills” — God is owner, not debtor, in every act of worship."

"“A thousand years… as yesterday” — a simile for God's eternity, not a formula for dating."

"“Rulers of thousands” — the thousand as a company of men under one captain."
